speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Hi everybody, Peter Zion coming to you from Washington, D.C. That's Mellon Auditorium behind me.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Today we're going to talk about an up-to-coming trip that Joe Biden has to Angola.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Now, during the Cold War, the United States and Angola were definitely on opposite sides.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: There was a civil war there that the Soviets and the Cubans and later the Chinese were supporting on one side.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: We were supporting on the—oh, hello, that's a big-ass squirrel that seems to think that I have food for it.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Huh. Anyway, during that time, so the Americans were on one side, the Soviets were on the other side,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: and American oil companies were helping the Soviet-backed government generate oil that was then sold to Europe,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: and, you know, Cold War, weird stuff.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Anyway, bottom line is that the Cold War is long since over, Americans are saying bygones,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: and the Angolans are a little curious as to the details, but they're open to some sort of a deal.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: It's not that Angola is all that important to the United States for its own sake.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: I mean, yes, they produce one and a half to two million barrels of crude a day,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: but the U.S. is the world's largest refined product exporter now and the world's largest crude producer,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: so it's not like we need it for us or even for our allies anymore.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: The issue has to do with mining.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Africa is kind of the great frontier for large-scale mining,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: particularly on a belt of countries going from Congo south.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: This is the old Cecil Rhodes route.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Cecil Rhodes is the guy who basically founded modern South Africa.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: And from the Copper Belt in southern Congo, there's a series of collection railroads that link together and form a spine

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: going down Zambia, Zimbabwe, Botswana, and ultimately reaching the better ports in South Africa.

speaker: SPEAKER_02
text: Well, there's something called the Benguela Roadway or the Lobito Corridor that cuts across Angola to the Atlantic that intersects this line.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: And ever since apartheid ended in South Africa, the government has become increasingly dysfunctional and the maintenance on the main spine railway has steadily degraded to the point that it's pretty rough in a lot of places.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: So, the idea the United States has is if we can rehabilitate the Lobito Corridor and rebuild the Benguela Railway, which dates back to the Portuguese occupation a century ago,

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: wow, then there's another route for this stuff to get out, and it would be going to the Atlantic instead of the Indian Ocean Basin,

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: and that's closer to the United States and Europe as opposed to China.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: So, it's become a bit of a tug of war that the Angolans are encouraging because everybody's spending infrastructure money in their country.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: And the people who won the Civil War, the pro-Soviet, are a minority.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: So, now we have the group that the United States used to support, which is closer to the majority, that's kind of an oppressed population.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: So, once again, there's all kinds of weird geopolitics going on in this southwest African nation.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: At this point, building the railway is pretty straightforward.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: The United States is basically invested in this project as one of its bigger overseas aid projects,

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: and it's probably going to be completed and operational within a couple of years.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: Too little, too late.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: Time will tell.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: But the country is very much in play.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: And so, of course, Uncle Joe's going there.
